artifact.self_contained_problem:
Algorithmic information theory studies the information content of finite and infinite binary strings via notions such as plain Kolmogorov complexity C(x) and prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity K(x), defined (up to an additive constant) as the length of a shortest (prefix-free) program that, when run on a fixed universal (prefix-free) Turing machine, outputs the string x; from these one derives concepts such as algorithmic randomness of infinite sequences (Martin-Löf randomness), mutual algorithmic information, algorithmic probability, and Chaitin's halting probability Ω.

Provide a formal axiomatic foundation for algorithmic information theory. More precisely, give a finite (or recursively enumerable) collection of axioms, formulated in a suitable formal language, such that:

(i) any function K : {0,1}* → ℕ (and the associated derived notions of randomness, information, and algorithmic probability) satisfying these axioms reproduces the standard theorems of algorithmic information theory (invariance theorem, coding theorem, symmetry of information, characterization of Martin-Löf random sequences, incompressibility properties, etc.);

(ii) the standard prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity (relative to a universal prefix-free machine) is a model of the axioms; and

(iii) the axiom system is categorical up to the natural equivalence (equality up to additive constants, or another precisely specified equivalence relation) on complexity functions.

State and justify such an axiomatization, or prove that no such axiomatization (with prescribed properties) exists.
artifact.status_search_result: An axiomatic approach to algorithmic information theory, based on Blum-style axioms, was developed by M. Burgin (presented by Kolmogorov, 1982) and has been extended in subsequent work, providing a framework that subsumes many specific complexity measures. However, no single universally accepted, categorical axiomatization of the full theory (including randomness, mutual information, and algorithmic probability) has been settled, so the problem in its open-ended form is best regarded as partially addressed rather than definitively solved.

status_evidence.title: Algorithmic information theory - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: An axiomatic approach to algorithmic information theory based on the Blum axioms was introduced by Mark Burgin in a paper presented for publication by Andrey Kolmogorov (Burgin 1982).
status_evidence.claim: A partial axiomatic approach via Blum-style axioms exists (Burgin 1982), addressing the problem in part.

status_evidence.title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: List of open problems in AIT including item suggesting axiomatization (H. Jürgensen).
status_evidence.claim: The axiomatization problem is listed among open problems in algorithmic information theory.
